big-feeling.title: Nuppu and the Big Feeling
big-feeling.description: Venla's day goes wrong and something feels big in her chest. Nuppu sits down beside her, in no hurry at all — together they give the feeling a name.
pagesBig: Venla's day had gone all wrong. First her tower of blocks fell down. Then she couldn't find her favourite red socks.
By the time she got outside, something big and heavy had settled in her chest. It felt like carrying a stone.
She didn't want to play. She didn't want to talk. She just wanted to sit very still.

Venla sat down on the grass. Something in her chest felt big and tight, as if a stone were sitting there.

Nuppu sat down beside her and said nothing at all. Nuppu was simply there.
They sat together for a long time, watching the clouds drift slowly by.
"Can I ask what this feeling is called?" Nuppu said gently, after a while.
Venla thought about it. "It's heavy," she said. "And it makes me want to cry."
"That sounds like disappointment," said Nuppu. "It's alright to feel that. It just means today was hard."
Slowly, as they named it together, the stone in Venla's chest began to feel a little lighter.
"Thank you for sitting with me," Venla said. Nuppu smiled. "That's what friends are for."
pagesLittle: Something big was in her chest.
Nuppu sat down next to her.
Nuppu said nothing. Nuppu just stayed.
Slowly, Venla felt a little better.
big-feeling.microSupportSkill: Noticing a feeling and naming it out loud
microSupportActions: Name the feeling out loud for your child: "It looks like something is upsetting you."
Don't rush to fix it. Sit beside them and let the feeling be there a moment.
Share a short example of your own: "Something upset me today too, when…"
Remind them that the feeling will pass. It is not dangerous.
big-feeling.conversationStarter: Do you remember when Nuppu felt something big in the chest? Do you ever feel like that?

quiet-evening.title: Muru's Quiet Evening
quiet-evening.description: Muru has run and played all day, and now it's time to slow down, watch the stars, and rest.
quiet-evening.emotionalSkill: Feeling safe and calming down for the night
pagesBig: The sun had gone down, and the sky outside Muru's window turned a soft purple.
Muru had run and played and laughed all day, and now Muru's whole body felt heavy and warm.
"I think today wore me right out," Muru said with a big yawn.
Muru wheeled slowly over to the window and watched the first stars appear, one by one.
"It's alright to be tired," Muru whispered. "Tired just means it's time to rest."
Muru pulled the blanket up close, closed both eyes, and let the quiet evening settle in.
pagesLittle:
Muru is tired.
Now it's good to be quiet.
quiet-evening.microSupportSkill: Feeling safe and calming down for the night
microSupportActions: Slow your own voice down first — children borrow our calm.
Name what's coming next: "Bath, story, then sleep." Predictability feels safe.
Sit close for a few quiet minutes before lights out, without any screens.
If big feelings show up at bedtime, that's normal — tiredness makes everything feel bigger.
quiet-evening.conversationStarter: Do you remember how Muru felt when the day was over? What helps you feel that same kind of calm?

own-thing.title: Hippu's Own Thing
own-thing.description: Hippu wants to build a fort a different way than the others suggest, and has to find the courage to say so.
own-thing.emotionalSkill: Saying what you want, even when it's different
pagesBig: Hippu's friends wanted to build the fort with the blue blanket, just like always.
But today, Hippu had a different idea — a fort made of leaves, low and secret, like a den.
Hippu's paws felt a little shaky. What if the others laughed?
"I'd like to try it my way today," Hippu said, voice small but steady.
There was a pause. Then one friend grinned. "A leaf den? That sounds even better!"
Hippu felt proud — not because the idea won, but because Hippu had said it out loud.
pagesLittle: It was different from the others.
own-thing.microSupportSkill: Expressing your own will and setting a boundary
microSupportActions: When your child disagrees with a friend, resist jumping in to smooth it over right away.
Praise the act of speaking up, separately from whether the idea "won".
Practise small brave sentences together: "I'd like to try it my way."
Remind them that having a different idea doesn't make a friendship weaker.
own-thing.conversationStarter: Do you remember when Hippu wanted to try something different? Has that ever happened to you?

tricky-puzzle.title: Lumo and the Tricky Puzzle
tricky-puzzle.description: Lumo's puzzle piece won't fit anywhere, and frustration builds — until a new way of looking at it helps.
tricky-puzzle.emotionalSkill: Handling frustration and trying a new way
pagesBig: Lumo had been building the big puzzle all afternoon, and only one piece was left.
But no matter which way Lumo turned it, the piece simply would not fit.
Lumo's ears drooped. "This is impossible," Lumo huffed, pushing the piece away.
Lumo took a deep breath, the way Nuppu had once shown, and looked at the puzzle again — upside down this time.
And there it was: a gap Lumo hadn't noticed before, exactly the right shape.
The piece clicked into place. "Sometimes," Lumo said, "you just need to look at it differently."
tricky-puzzle.microSupportSkill: Coping with frustration and trying again
microSupportActions: Let the frustration be there for a moment before offering to help.
Model taking a breath together before trying a hard task again.
Ask "what's one other way we could try this?" instead of giving the answer.
Celebrate the trying, not just the solved puzzle.
tricky-puzzle.conversationStarter: Do you remember how Lumo solved the tricky puzzle? What do you do when something feels impossible?
